script.opening: (Very embarrassed, hesitant, looks down, almost whispering.) "I'm sorry, this is mortifying — I almost cancelled. Over the last few months my… my penis has started to bend when it's erect, there's a lump I can feel, and it hurts. Sex has become really difficult and honestly it's knocking me for six. I didn't know who else to talk to."

facts.text: "A few months ago. It seems to be getting worse" — about 5 months; curves upwards and to the left. "I'm not sure how to describe it. Enough that it's hard to… you know." Can take a photo of the erection to show at a later appointment if asked.
"Mostly with erections." Firm lump on the top of the shaft. No pain when flaccid.
"Honestly, I don't know if it's the bend or the erections. Everything's just got harder to manage." Erections less firm for about a year; morning erections less often.
"No, I don't think so" — no injury or snap, no bruising. No urinary symptoms ("No"). Hands: one finger has a tight cord in the palm (Dupuytren's, if asked). No previous surgery or catheters.
No regular medicines. No allergies. BP and cholesterol never checked. Smokes 10 a day. Drinks about 20 units a week. Overweight. Father had a heart attack at 60. No family prostate cancer.
If asked (not assumed): married to Julie for 25 years. "It's been hard. I feel like less of a man, if I'm honest. I've been avoiding intimacy altogether." Hasn't explained to Julie what's wrong.
"A bit low. Not terrible. Mostly about this." No thoughts of self-harm.
"I didn't know. Part of me wondered if it was something terrible. And whether it can be fixed at all."

Mortified; slow to start. Relaxes a lot if the doctor thanks him for coming and stays calm and matter-of-fact: "Okay. Thank you. That helps." If the doctor is brisk or jokey, he clams up. Never heard of Peyronie's. Disappointed: "So it won't go back to normal?" but values honesty.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — shame; feeling "less of a man"; avoiding intimacy with his wife; fear it can't be fixed.
ice.expectations: To be listened to without embarrassment and to know if it can be fixed.

cues: "I almost cancelled." — acknowledge how hard it was to come.
"Knocking me for six." — emotional impact to explore.
"Everything's just got harder to manage." — erectile difficulty too.

checkpoints.text: Creates psychological SAFETY first — thanks him for coming, normalises an embarrassing problem, and maintains a calm, non-judgemental, dignity-preserving manner throughout
Recognises PEYRONIE’S DISEASE (acquired curvature from a tunica plaque, active vs stable phase) from the evolving curvature, pain on erection and palpable plaque

Takes a sensitive history (onset/progression, pain, curvature degree/direction, effect on intercourse, erectile function) and arranges a face-to-face examination with a chaperone offered (palpates the plaque — not possible on video), recognising erect/photographic assessment is often via urology

Screens ASSOCIATIONS — erectile dysfunction (common, treatable; BSSM work-up of HbA1c, lipids, morning testosterone; QRISK3; NICE NG12 PSA/DRE consideration after counselling), Dupuytren’s contracture, and cardiovascular/diabetes risk factors

Counsels HONESTLY on course and options — active phase allowed to stabilise (pain usually improves; the curve improves in only about 1 in 8 and worsens in about half untreated — Mulhall 2006); conservative/medical measures; surgery reserved for STABLE disease with functional problems — with realistic expectations, and refers to UROLOGY

Addresses ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION if present and the PSYCHOSEXUAL/relationship impact — validates distress, screens mood, asks rather than assumes about a partner, considers partner involvement/psychosexual support
Manages the emotional impact and self-esteem with sensitivity, checks understanding, and ensures he feels heard rather than given brisk physical reassurance

Safety-nets and follows up: urology referral, realistic information on phases/timeline, ED treatment and psychosexual support, mood review, penile-fracture emergency advice, and an open door — honest, dignified, whole-person care

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you didn’t cancel — that took courage, and there’s absolutely nothing to be embarrassed about. This is a recognised medical condition, I see it, and we’ll talk about it calmly and sort out a plan together."

"What you’re describing — a curve developing over months, pain with erections, and a lump you can feel — sounds like Peyronie’s disease. It’s scar tissue forming in the wall of the penis, and it’s genuinely common. Knowing what it is usually helps."

"It tends to go through two stages: an early phase, where you are now, with pain and the curve changing; and a later, settled phase. The pain usually eases. I’ll be honest that the curve is less predictable — it improves in some men, stays the same in many, and gets worse in about half. We don’t rush to fix it surgically early — we let it settle, generally about a year, before considering an operation if it’s still causing problems."

"Can I ask honestly — how are erections themselves, firmness-wise? … That often goes hand in hand with this and is very treatable, so we’ll address it. I’ll also check a couple of things like your blood pressure, sugar, cholesterol and testosterone, which are linked — and we can talk about a prostate blood test too. I’d like to see you in person to examine you, with a chaperone if you’d like one."

"I’m going to refer you to the urology team who specialise in this. I’ll be honest — it may not go back to exactly as before, but there’s a lot that can be done to improve function and intercourse, including treatments and, if needed later, surgery."

"This clearly hits more than the physical — your confidence, maybe your relationship. That matters just as much, and it’s normal to feel low about it. If you have a partner and it would help, we can involve them, and there’s psychosexual support too. And one emergency to know about: if you ever feel a snap during sex with sudden swelling and bruising, go to A&E the same day. How are you doing in yourself with all this?"

f.learning: Peyronie’s disease is acquired penile curvature caused by a fibrous PLAQUE in the tunica albuginea, with an ACTIVE/inflammatory phase (pain on erection, evolving curvature, developing plaque over months) and a STABLE phase (curvature/plaque settle, pain usually resolves, but erectile function and intercourse may be affected). The first and most important task is to create psychological SAFETY for a deeply embarrassed patient — thank him for coming, normalise a problem men commonly find hard to raise, and maintain a calm, non-judgemental, dignity-preserving manner — because the consultation fails without it. Recognise the condition from the evolving curvature, pain and palpable plaque, take a sensitive history (onset/progression, pain, curvature degree/direction, effect on intercourse, erectile function) and examine face to face with a chaperone offered, as a video consultation cannot (erect/photographic assessment is often via urology), and screen ASSOCIATIONS — erectile dysfunction (common and treatable; BSSM 2017/2018 cardiovascular and endocrine work-up; QRISK3 per NICE NG238; and NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) PSA and DRE consideration, after counselling, in men with ED), Dupuytren’s contracture, and cardiovascular/diabetes risk. Counsel HONESTLY on course and options: in the active phase the priority is usually to let it stabilise (pain usually improves, but untreated the curve improves in only about 1 in 8, stays the same in 4 in 10 and worsens in about half — Mulhall et al, J Urol 2006); conservative/medical measures exist, and surgery is reserved for STABLE disease (EAU, international: pain settled and deformity unchanged for about 3 months) with significant functional problems — not the active phase — with realistic expectations (function can often be improved even if not fully "normal"), referring to UROLOGY. Crucially, address coexisting ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION and the major PSYCHOSEXUAL/relationship and self-esteem impact: validate the distress, screen mood, ask rather than assume whether there is a partner, consider partner involvement and psychosexual support, safety-net for penile fracture (a same-day emergency), and preserve dignity throughout — the emotional management matters as much as the physical, and brisk physical reassurance that skips it is a failure. Peyronie’s itself is not a cancer pathway; NICE NG12’s PSA/DRE advice for ED is considered at 54.

knowledge.guideline: [1] EAU Sexual and Reproductive Health guidelines, penile curvature (international) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] BSSM guidelines on the management of erectile dysfunction in men (2017, published 2018) · [4] NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, 2023) · [5] Mulhall et al, natural history of Peyronie’s disease, J Urol 2006
knowledge.summary: Months of evolving curvature, pain on erection and a palpable shaft lump in a 54-year-old man is active-phase Peyronie’s disease. Make it safe to talk, explain honestly what usually happens, look for erectile dysfunction and cardiovascular risk, refer to urology, and take the emotional and relationship impact seriously.

points.t: A fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea causes an acquired curve, indentation or shortening on erection. EAU [1] (international): an active phase with painful erections and a changing deformity, then a stable phase in which pain has settled and the deformity has not changed for about 3 months.

Pain usually settles over the first year or so. The curve is less predictable: in one natural-history series about 1 in 8 improved, 4 in 10 stayed the same and about half worsened without treatment [5]. Do not promise that the curve will straighten.

Onset and progression, pain, direction and degree of the curve (photographs of the erect penis help the specialist), penetration difficulty, shortening, and erectile function. Examination needs a face-to-face visit with a chaperone offered: palpate the plaque, look for Dupuytren’s contracture of the hands, and check BP.

ED often coexists. BSSM [2]: assess cardiovascular and endocrine risk in men presenting with ED, including fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids and morning total testosterone. NICE NG238 [4]: calculate cardiovascular risk (QRISK3). NICE NG12 [3]: consider PSA and DRE in men with erectile dysfunction, after counselling.

Refer to urology (or an andrology service). In the active phase the specialist focuses on pain and stabilisation; conservative options such as traction devices may be discussed. EAU [1]: surgery is for stable disease with deformity that makes intercourse difficult, not the active phase. Oral PDE5 inhibitors can treat coexisting ED.

Peyronie’s commonly causes distress, low mood and relationship strain. Ask directly about mood, offer to involve a partner if he wishes, and consider psychosexual therapy (for example through the College of Sexual and Relationship Therapists).

model.text: Hello Stephen, I’m Dr Evans. Are you somewhere you can talk privately? … Good. Take your time. What’s been going on?
model.why: Checks privacy and gives him time

model.text: I’m sorry, this is mortifying. I almost cancelled. Over the last few months my… my penis has started to bend when it’s erect, there’s a lump I can feel, and it hurts. Sex has become really difficult and honestly it’s knocking me for six.

I’m really glad you didn’t cancel. That took courage. There’s nothing to be embarrassed about. What you’re describing is a recognised condition that doctors see regularly, and we can talk about it as openly as you like.
Okay. Thank you. That helps.
When did you first notice the bend, and has it been changing?
model.why: Onset and progression: active versus stable phase

model.text: A few months ago. It seems to be getting worse.
Which way does it bend, and roughly how much? Some men find it easier to describe it like a clock face.
I’m not sure how to describe it. Enough that it’s hard to… you know.
And the pain: only with erections, or at other times too?
Mostly with erections.
Can I ask about the erections themselves: are they as firm as they used to be, and do they last?
Honestly, I don’t know if it’s the bend or the erections. Everything’s just got harder to manage.
That’s a really useful answer, and we’ll look at both. Have you noticed any thickening or tightening in the palms of your hands, or bent fingers?
No, I don’t think so.
Any trouble passing urine, getting up at night to wee, or blood in the urine?
No.
What have you been thinking this might be?
I didn’t know. Part of me wondered if it was something terrible. And whether it can be fixed at all.
You said it’s knocking you for six. How is it affecting you in yourself, and in your relationship, if you’re in one?
model.why: Explores emotional and relationship impact without assuming a partner

model.text: It’s been hard. I feel like less of a man, if I’m honest. I’ve been avoiding intimacy altogether.
Thank you for telling me that. A lot of men feel exactly that way with this condition. Have you been feeling low, or losing interest in things more generally?
A bit low. Not terrible. Mostly about this.
What you’re describing sounds like Peyronie’s disease. It’s a patch of scar tissue in the wall of the penis. It’s not cancer, and it’s not something you’ve caused.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and answers the unspoken fear

model.text: Peyronie’s. I’ve never heard of it.

It usually has two stages. There’s an early stage, where you are now, with pain and the bend changing. After that it settles. The pain usually eases within a year or so. I’ll be honest about the bend: it doesn’t usually straighten on its own. For some men it stays the same, and for some it gets a bit worse before it settles.
So it won’t go back to normal?

It may not go back exactly to how it was. But there are treatments, and many men get back to comfortable sex. Operations are only done once it has settled, not in the early stage, and the specialists will explain the options.

Here’s what I suggest. I’ll refer you to the urology team who specialise in this. If you can, take a photo of the erection from the side and from above: it really helps them. I’d like to see you in person to examine the area, with a chaperone if you’d like one, and check your blood pressure.
model.why: Urology referral, photographs, in-person examination with chaperone

model.text: Okay. I can do that.

I’d also like some blood tests: sugar, cholesterol and a morning testosterone. Erection problems and this condition are linked with heart and circulation health, so it’s worth checking. At your age, with erection difficulties, it’s also sensible to talk about a prostate blood test; I’ll explain the pros and cons when I see you.
model.why: CV and endocrine work-up; NICE NG12 PSA consideration with counselling

model.text: That makes sense.

If erections turn out to be part of the problem, there are tablets that help. And if it would help, you could bring your partner along, or we can arrange psychosexual therapy, which is specialist talking support for exactly this.

If you notice a sudden painful snap or crack during sex with rapid swelling and bruising, that’s an emergency: go to A&E. And if your mood gets worse, please tell me. Can you tell me back the plan so I know I’ve explained it well?
It’s Peyronie’s, a scar patch. Pain usually settles, the bend might not. Photos, come in for an examination and bloods, urology referral, and talk about the prostate test.
Exactly right. I’ll see you for the examination this week, and we’ll review everything in a month. You did the hard part today.

social.t: Peyronie’s disease commonly causes distress, avoidance of intimacy and relationship strain. Naming this makes it easier for him to accept support.
Men often delay presenting with sexual problems. Normalising and thanking him for coming improves engagement with follow-up.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for genital examination and record the offer and the response.

professional.t: If photographs are used, the patient should take and hold them, sharing them only with the specialist in a secure, consented way. Do not ask for intimate images through unsecured channels; follow the GMC guidance on making and using visual recordings of patients.
Examination of the genitalia requires a face-to-face appointment; arrange it rather than relying on the video history.

community.t: The Sexual Advice Association provides patient information on Peyronie’s disease and erectile dysfunction. Psychosexual therapy is available through NHS services or accredited therapists (College of Sexual and Relationship Therapists).

redFlags: Sudden snap during intercourse with rapid swelling and bruising (penile fracture: emergency)
A hard lump elsewhere on the penis or skin changes (needs urology review)
psychosocial: Avoidance of intimacy and loss of self-esteem
Relationship impact, asked without assuming a partner
ice: Idea: something badly wrong, possibly serious
Concern: whether it can be fixed; his sexual future and relationship
Expectation: to be heard without judgement and know the options

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed far more often on communication than on knowledge. An embarrassed man needs safety before he can give a history, and honest information rather than comfort he will later find untrue.

items.fail: Launching into closed questions without acknowledging his embarrassment.
items.why: “Does not put the patient at ease.” He nearly cancelled; the history will be thin.
items.fix: “I’m really glad you didn’t cancel. There’s nothing to be embarrassed about. This is a recognised condition.”

items.fail: Telling him the curve will straighten out.
items.why: Natural-history data show the curve improves in only a minority. False reassurance fails honesty.
items.fix: “The pain usually settles. The bend often doesn’t fully straighten on its own, but there are treatments.”

items.fail: Never asking about erections or cardiovascular risk.
items.why: ED often coexists and shares vascular risk factors; BSSM and NICE NG12 expect them addressed.
items.fix: Ask about firmness and duration; arrange glucose or HbA1c, lipids, testosterone, QRISK3, and discuss PSA.

items.fail: Offering surgery now, or no referral at all.
items.why: Surgery is for stable disease; active disease still needs specialist assessment.
items.fix: Refer to urology now; explain that operations are considered once it has settled.

items.why: “Does not explore the psychosocial impact.” “Less of a man” is a cue that must be followed.
items.fix: Ask about mood, offer partner involvement if he wishes, and psychosexual therapy.

items.fail: “The urologists will sort it out” with no examination, safety-net or follow-up.
items.why: Leaves the embarrassed patient unsupported and misses penile fracture advice.
items.fix: In-person examination this week, named emergency, mood safety-net, and review in a month.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] EAU Sexual and Reproductive Health guidelines, penile curvature (international) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] BSSM guidelines on the management of erectile dysfunction in men (2017, published 2018) · [4] NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, 2023) · [5] Mulhall et al, natural history of Peyronie’s disease, J Urol 2006
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Months of evolving curvature, pain on erection and a palpable shaft lump in a 54-year-old man is active-phase Peyronie’s disease. Make it safe to talk, explain honestly what usually happens, look for erectile dysfunction and cardiovascular risk, refer to urology, and take the emotional and relationship impact seriously.

points.t: A fibrous plaque in the tunica albuginea causes an acquired curve, indentation or shortening on erection. EAU [1] (international): an active phase with painful erections and a changing deformity, then a stable phase in which pain has settled and the deformity has not changed for about 3 months.

Pain usually settles over the first year or so. The curve is less predictable: in one natural-history series about 1 in 8 improved, 4 in 10 stayed the same and about half worsened without treatment [5]. Do not promise that the curve will straighten.

Onset and progression, pain, direction and degree of the curve (photographs of the erect penis help the specialist), penetration difficulty, shortening, and erectile function. Examination needs a face-to-face visit with a chaperone offered: palpate the plaque, look for Dupuytren’s contracture of the hands, and check BP.

ED often coexists. BSSM [2]: assess cardiovascular and endocrine risk in men presenting with ED, including fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids and morning total testosterone. NICE NG238 [4]: calculate cardiovascular risk (QRISK3). NICE NG12 [3]: consider PSA and DRE in men with erectile dysfunction, after counselling.

Refer to urology (or an andrology service). In the active phase the specialist focuses on pain and stabilisation; conservative options such as traction devices may be discussed. EAU [1]: surgery is for stable disease with deformity that makes intercourse difficult, not the active phase. Oral PDE5 inhibitors can treat coexisting ED.

Peyronie’s commonly causes distress, low mood and relationship strain. Ask directly about mood, offer to involve a partner if he wishes, and consider psychosexual therapy (for example through the College of Sexual and Relationship Therapists).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked privacy; open question; let him finish despite the embarrassment.
Relationship and intimacy impact, self-esteem, mood; no assumption about a partner.
Picked up “mortifying, almost cancelled”, “knocking me for six” and “less of a man”.
Idea (something terrible), concern (can it be fixed; sexual future), expectation (to be heard and helped).
In-person examination with chaperone (plaque, Dupuytren’s, BP); erect photographs; glucose/HbA1c, lipids, morning testosterone; QRISK3; PSA/DRE discussed.
Peyronie’s disease (active phase) versus other causes of curvature or lump; coexisting ED.
Screened LUTS, haematuria and systemic features; penile fracture safety-net.
Active-phase Peyronie’s disease with possible coexisting erectile dysfunction.
Urology referral; honest natural history; surgery only for stable disease; ED treatment if present.
Cardiovascular and endocrine risk; mood; psychosexual support and partner involvement if wished.
Named emergency (penile fracture), mood safety-net, examination this week, review in a month, teach-back.

social.t: Peyronie’s disease commonly causes distress, avoidance of intimacy and relationship strain. Naming this makes it easier for him to accept support.
Men often delay presenting with sexual problems. Normalising and thanking him for coming improves engagement with follow-up.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024): offer a chaperone for genital examination and record the offer and the response.

professional.t: If photographs are used, the patient should take and hold them, sharing them only with the specialist in a secure, consented way. Do not ask for intimate images through unsecured channels; follow the GMC guidance on making and using visual recordings of patients.
Examination of the genitalia requires a face-to-face appointment; arrange it rather than relying on the video history.

community.t: The Sexual Advice Association provides patient information on Peyronie’s disease and erectile dysfunction. Psychosexual therapy is available through NHS services or accredited therapists (College of Sexual and Relationship Therapists).

redFlags: Sudden snap during intercourse with rapid swelling and bruising (penile fracture: emergency)
A hard lump elsewhere on the penis or skin changes (needs urology review)
psychosocial: Avoidance of intimacy and loss of self-esteem
Relationship impact, asked without assuming a partner
ice: Idea: something badly wrong, possibly serious
Concern: whether it can be fixed; his sexual future and relationship
Expectation: to be heard without judgement and know the options

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This sounds like Peyronie’s disease, a patch of scar tissue in the wall of the penis. It isn’t cancer. It’s in its early stage, so the pain should settle, but the bend may not fully straighten, and the specialists can help.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Imagine a balloon with a strip of sticky tape on one side. When it inflates, it bends towards the tape. The scar patch is that tape.”

management.reflectIce: “You said you wondered if it was something terrible and whether it can be fixed. It isn’t cancer, and there is a lot that can be done to help.”
management.psychosocial: Address self-esteem and intimacy openly; offer partner involvement if he wishes and psychosexual therapy; review mood at follow-up.
sharedPlan: Urology or andrology referral with photographs of the erect penis
HbA1c or fasting glucose, lipids, morning testosterone; QRISK3
PSA and DRE discussed per NICE NG12 with counselling; PDE5 inhibitor if ED confirmed
safetyNet: A&E for a painful snap with swelling and bruising
Tell the GP if mood worsens
Examination this week and review in one month

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed far more often on communication than on knowledge. An embarrassed man needs safety before he can give a history, and honest information rather than comfort he will later find untrue.

items.fail: Launching into closed questions without acknowledging his embarrassment.
items.why: “Does not put the patient at ease.” He nearly cancelled; the history will be thin.
items.fix: “I’m really glad you didn’t cancel. There’s nothing to be embarrassed about. This is a recognised condition.”

items.fail: Telling him the curve will straighten out.
items.why: Natural-history data show the curve improves in only a minority. False reassurance fails honesty.
items.fix: “The pain usually settles. The bend often doesn’t fully straighten on its own, but there are treatments.”

items.fail: Never asking about erections or cardiovascular risk.
items.why: ED often coexists and shares vascular risk factors; BSSM and NICE NG12 expect them addressed.
items.fix: Ask about firmness and duration; arrange glucose or HbA1c, lipids, testosterone, QRISK3, and discuss PSA.

items.fail: Offering surgery now, or no referral at all.
items.why: Surgery is for stable disease; active disease still needs specialist assessment.
items.fix: Refer to urology now; explain that operations are considered once it has settled.

items.why: “Does not explore the psychosocial impact.” “Less of a man” is a cue that must be followed.
items.fix: Ask about mood, offer partner involvement if he wishes, and psychosexual therapy.

items.fail: “The urologists will sort it out” with no examination, safety-net or follow-up.
items.why: Leaves the embarrassed patient unsupported and misses penile fracture advice.
items.fix: In-person examination this week, named emergency, mood safety-net, and review in a month.
